terms.definition: The discount supermarket chain the game is set in: about 1200 stores, a small core range, and a middle aisle promotion that rotates every week.
terms.why_it_matters: Every stakeholder, every metric and every trade-off in this project is downstream of how this chain actually runs.

terms.definition: Lindenmarkt's demand forecasting and replenishment platform. Every night it forecasts demand for every article in every store and turns that into order suggestions for the distribution centres.
terms.why_it_matters: This is the system the player is here to run. Every challenge in the game is a decision about what Shelfcast should do next.

terms.definition: A honey vault watched over by Bear Bruce and audited by Mohawk Mark - the standalone practice scenario for the introduction, with nothing to do with Lindenmarkt or Shelfcast.
terms.why_it_matters: It exists so the game's mechanics can be learned on something with no stakes, before anything here counts against the real project that follows.

terms.definition: Money the chain has already promised and cannot get back, such as a supplier order signed before a single unit has sold.
terms.why_it_matters: It is what turns a forecast into a decision somebody is answerable for. Nobody argues this hard about a number that costs nothing to be wrong about.

terms.definition: What is left of a sale after what the goods cost, and the number a buyer is measured on.
terms.why_it_matters: Whenever a stakeholder talks about business value here, this is usually what they mean underneath it.

terms.definition: Cutting the price to move stock that is not selling at the price it was set at.
terms.why_it_matters: What a bad forecast costs, paid in margin. It is also a change in the data: the sales that follow were bought by the price, not by demand.

terms.definition: More of an article than the shelf and the coming days can absorb, wherever it is sitting.
terms.why_it_matters: Not free to hold: it takes shelf space from something that would have sold, and on fresh articles it is waste with a delay.

terms.definition: Promotional articles still sitting in the warehouse or the store when the promotion week ends.
terms.why_it_matters: The specific failure mode of the middle aisle: it does not spoil, it just occupies a warehouse and someone's budget until it is marked down.

terms.definition: Stock that disappears without being sold, through theft, breakage or miscounting.
terms.why_it_matters: It quietly widens the gap between recorded stock and the real shelf, which means the system is forecasting against a number that is already wrong.

terms.definition: Fresh articles thrown away because they passed their date before anyone bought them.
terms.why_it_matters: The other number the project is judged on, and the one that pulls every decision towards ordering less. Availability and waste are the same dial.

terms.definition: One sellable product as the chain's systems know it, identified by its own number.
terms.why_it_matters: The unit everything is counted in: a forecast is made per article, per store, per day.

terms.definition: The person who chooses the promotional articles, negotiates with suppliers and commits the purchase quantity for the whole chain.
terms.why_it_matters: The buyer is the one the forecast is trying to help, and the one whose judgement it is quietly replacing.

terms.definition: The team that owns a slice of the range, deciding what it contains, what it costs and when it is promoted.
terms.why_it_matters: They own the calendar the whole project has to fit inside.

terms.definition: The roughly 2000 everyday articles a store always carries, as opposed to the promotions that come and go.
terms.why_it_matters: The core range is where availability and waste are won or lost every single day, quietly, without anyone advertising it.

terms.definition: The weekly printed advertisement that announces the promotion, committed to print days before the articles reach the shelf.
terms.why_it_matters: Printing turns a forecast into a public promise. Once an article is in the leaflet, running out is a complaint rather than a miss.

terms.definition: The rotating non-food promotion that sits in the centre of the store: around 80 seasonal articles that appear for one week, are advertised in the leaflet, and are never restocked once they sell out.
terms.why_it_matters: One shot, no second delivery. Every middle aisle forecast is a bet placed weeks ahead that cannot be corrected on the day.

terms.definition: The week a particular set of promotional articles is on sale, fixed in the calendar long before it starts.
terms.why_it_matters: The date does not move. Anything the team wants to change has to be ready before the leaflet goes to print.

terms.definition: Everything bought together in one transaction.
terms.why_it_matters: Baskets show what moves together, which is how a promotion is credited with sales that happened elsewhere in the store.

terms.definition: The chain's shopper app, which ties baskets to a person and carries consent and retention obligations as a result.
terms.why_it_matters: The only personal data in the project. It is why governance stakeholders have something real to defend rather than paperwork to cite.

terms.definition: One line of a receipt: which article, how many, at what price, in which store, at what time.
terms.why_it_matters: The raw material of the whole system. A night of missing scan lines is a night of demand the model will never learn about.

terms.definition: The reference records describing stores, suppliers and articles: size, region, opening hours, pack sizes, lead times.
terms.why_it_matters: Slow moving, rarely owned by anybody in the room, and wrong often enough to explain a forecast nobody can otherwise explain.

terms.definition: The checkout where a sale is recorded, one scanned article at a time.
terms.why_it_matters: Everything the system knows about demand starts here, which is why an article that never reached the shelf is invisible to it.

terms.definition: A bought in forecast of temperature and conditions per region, used for fresh produce and seasonal promotions.
terms.why_it_matters: An outside dependency nobody in the team controls, arriving daily, capable of moving demand more than anything the team does.

terms.definition: How often a shopper finds what they came for on the shelf, measured across articles and stores.
terms.why_it_matters: One of the two numbers the project is judged on, and the one that pulls every decision towards ordering more.

terms.definition: The short window each morning in which stores must send their orders for the day.
terms.why_it_matters: A forecast that finishes late is a forecast that did not happen. Stores fall back to last week's numbers and order blind.

terms.definition: An article a shopper came for and did not find, because the shelf was empty when they reached it.
terms.why_it_matters: It is also a hole in the data: once an article is gone the tills stop recording demand that was still there.

terms.definition: A store manager changing the quantity the system suggested before the order goes out.
terms.why_it_matters: The team's honest measure of trust. A model can be accurate and still be overridden into irrelevance.

terms.definition: What is really in the store, as opposed to what the system believes is there.
terms.why_it_matters: The two drift apart through breakage, theft and miscounts, and every order suggestion is computed from the belief rather than from the shelf.

terms.definition: How much of an article physically fits in its place on the shelf.
terms.why_it_matters: A perfect order is still wrong if the delivery does not fit. Capacity is the constraint that turns a number into a pallet in a corridor.

terms.definition: The person running one store, who sees the suggested order each morning and can change it before it is sent.
terms.why_it_matters: They are the last human in the loop and the only one who can see the shelf. Their overrides are the system's report card.

terms.definition: Dividing a fixed quantity of promotional stock between stores before any of it has sold.
terms.why_it_matters: Unlike replenishment there is nothing to learn from as you go. The split is decided once, on a forecast, and then lived with.

terms.definition: Buying a large quantity in one commitment, usually for a better unit price, usually for a promotion.
terms.why_it_matters: The discount is real and so is the exposure. A bulk order is the forecast and the liability arriving at the same time.

terms.definition: The regional warehouse that receives goods from suppliers and sends each store what it ordered.
terms.why_it_matters: Stores do not order from suppliers, they order from here, which is where a forecast turns into a truck load.

terms.definition: The record a store makes when a delivery arrives and is booked into its stock.
terms.why_it_matters: A late or skipped receipt makes the system think the shelf is emptier than it is, and the next order compounds the error.

terms.definition: How long it takes between placing an order with a supplier and the goods arriving.
terms.why_it_matters: It sets how far ahead the forecast has to see. A long lead time means committing before you know anything useful.

terms.definition: The smallest amount a supplier will accept on an order, fixed by contract.
terms.why_it_matters: The reason a perfectly good forecast can be impossible to act on. The model asks for 40, the contract sells in 500.

terms.definition: The quantity the system proposes a store should order, produced from the forecast and the stock it already holds.
terms.why_it_matters: A suggestion, not an order. What separates the two is whether the store manager believes it.

terms.definition: The unit goods physically move in, which is rarely the unit a shopper buys in.
terms.why_it_matters: Forecasts come out in single articles and orders go in whole pallets. Somebody has to round, and rounding is where waste starts.

terms.definition: Refilling a store's shelves with what it has sold, as an ongoing cycle rather than a one off order.
terms.why_it_matters: This is the thing being automated. Everything the team argues about is downstream of getting it right.

terms.definition: Stock held deliberately above the forecast, to absorb the days when demand or delivery does not behave.
terms.why_it_matters: The dial between availability and waste, set by hand. Raising it hides a bad forecast and pays for the cover in stock nobody sold.

terms.definition: What the system believes a store currently holds, from deliveries received minus what the tills have sold.
terms.why_it_matters: A belief, not a fact. It drifts away from the real shelf through breakage, theft and miscounts, and the order suggestion never knows.

terms.definition: The manufacturer or wholesaler a buyer commits an order to, under contract terms that fix quantities and timing.
terms.why_it_matters: A committed supplier order is money already spent. It is the hardest constraint in the game, and no model argues with it.

terms.definition: One delivery run from the distribution centre to the stores, loaded against orders that closed earlier that day.
terms.why_it_matters: "Before the trucks leave" is the real deadline in this project. It is when a forecast stops being adjustable and becomes a load on a vehicle.
